As soon as he had stuffed himself with a host of good dishes, he began to leap and spring, to laugh and to fart like a little ass well stuffed with barley. Then he set to beating me with all his heart, shouting, "Slave! slave!" Lysistratus, as soon as he saw him, let fly this comparison at him. "Old fellow," said he, "you resemble one of the scum assuming the airs of a rich man or a stupid ass that has broken loose from its stable." "As for you," bawled the other at the top of his voice, "you are like a grasshopper, whose cloak is worn to the thread, or like Sthenelus after his clothes had been sold." All applauded excepting Theophrastus, who made a grimace as behoved a well-bred man like him. The old man called to him, "Hi! tell me then what you have to be proud of? Not so much mouthing, you, who so well know how to play the buffoon and to lick-spittle the rich!" In this way he insulted each in turn with the grossest of jests, and he reeled off a thousand of the most absurd and ridiculous speeches. At last, when he was thoroughly drunk, he started towards here, striking everyone he met. Wait, here he comes reeling along. I will be off for fear of his blows.

div.stage: Philocleon enters, inebriated and hilarious, carrying a torch; his other hand is occupied with a wholly nude flute-girl; he is followed by a group of angry victims of his exuberance.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Halt! and let everyone begone, or I shall do an evil turn to some of those who insist on following me. Clear off, rascals, or I shall roast you with this torch!

sp.speaker: Guest
sp.p: We shall all make you smart to-morrow for your youthful pranks. We shall come in a body to summon you to justice.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Ho! ho! summon me? what old women's babble! Know that I can no longer bear to hear even the name of suits. Ha! ha! ha! this is what pleases me, "Down with the urns!" Get out of here! Down with the dicasts! away with them, away with them!

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.stage: Dropping into speech; to the flute-girl
sp.p: Mount up there, my little gilded cock-chafer; take hold of this rope's end in your hand. Hold it tight, but have a care; the rope's a bit old and worn. But even though it's worn, it still has its virtues. Do you see how opportunely I got you away from the solicitations of those fellators, who wanted you to make love to them in their own odd way? You therefore owe me this return to gratify me. But will you pay the debt? Oh! I know well you will not even try; you will play with me, you will laugh heartily at me as you have done at many another man. And yet, if you would not be a naughty girl, I would redeem you, when my son is dead, and you should be my concubine, my little one. At present I am not my own master; I am very young and am watched very closely. My dear son never lets me out of his sight; he's an unbearable creature, who would quarter a thread and skin a flint; he is afraid I should get lost, for I am his only father. But here he comes running towards us. But be quick, don't stir, hold these torches. I am going to play him a young man's trick, the same as he played me before I was initiated into the mysteries.

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: Oh! oh! you debauched old dotard! you are amorous, it seems, of pretty baggages; but, by Apollo, it shall not be with impunity!

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Ah! you would be very glad to eat a lawsuit in vinegar, you would.

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: Only a rascal would steal the flute-girl away from the other guests.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: What flute-girl? Are you distraught, as if you had just returned from Pluto?

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: By Zeus! But here is the Dardanian wench in person.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Nonsense. This is a torch that I have lit in the public square in honour of the gods.

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: Is this a torch?

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: A torch? Certainly. Do you not see it is of several different colours?

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: And what is that black part in the middle?

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: That's the pitch running out while it burns.

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: And there, on the other side, surely that is a girl's bottom?

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: No. That's just a small bit of the torch, that projects.

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: What do you mean? what bit? Hi! you woman! come here!

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Oh! What do you want to do?

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: To take her away from you and lead her off. You are too much worn out and can do nothing.

div.stage: He takes the girl into the house.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Listen to me! One day, at Olympia, I saw Euphudion boxing bravely against Ascondas; he was already aged, and yet with a blow from his fist he knocked down his young opponent. So watch out that I don't blacken your eyes.

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: By Zeus! you have Olympia at your finger-ends!

div.stage: A Baker's Wife enters with an empty basket; she brings Chaerephon with her as witness.

sp.speaker: Baker's Wife
sp.p: Come to my help, I beg you, in the name of the gods! This cursed man, when striking out right and left with his torch, knocked over ten loaves worth an obolus apiece, and then, to cap the deal, four others.

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: Do you see what lawsuits you are drawing upon yourself with your drunkenness? You will have to plead.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Oh, no, no! a little pretty talk and pleasant tales will soon settle the matter and reconcile her with me.

sp.speaker: Baker's Wife
sp.p: Not so, by the goddesses twain! It shall not be said that you have with impunity spoilt the wares of Myrtia, the daughter of Ancylion and Sostrates.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Listen, woman, I wish to tell you a lovely anecdote.

sp.speaker: Baker's Wife
sp.p: By Zeus, no anecdotes for me, thank you.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: One night Aesop was going out to supper. A drunken bitch had the impudence to bark near him. Aesop said to her, "Oh, bitch, bitch! you would do well to sell your wicked tongue and buy some wheat."

sp.speaker: Baker's Wife
sp.p: You make a mock of me! Very well! I don't care who you are, I shall summons you before the market inspectors for damage done to my business. Chaerephon here shall be my witness.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: But just listen, here's another will perhaps please you better. Lasus and Simonides were contesting against each other for the singing prize. Lasus said, "Damned if I care."

sp.speaker: Baker's Wife
sp.p: Ah! really, did he now!

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: As for you, Chaerephon, can you be witness to this woman, who looks as pale and tragic as Ino when she throws herself from her rock ... at the feet of Euripides?

div.stage: The Baker's Wife and Chaerephon depart.

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: Here, I suppose, comes another to summons you; he has his witness too. Ah! unhappy indeed we are!

div.stage: A badly bruised man enters.

sp.speaker: Accuser
sp.p: I summons you, old man, for outrage.

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: For outrage? Oh! in the name of the gods, do not summons him! I will be answerable for him; name the price and I will be more more grateful still.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: I ask for nothing better than to be reconciled with him; for I admit I struck him and threw stones at him. So, first come here. Will you leave it in my hands to name the indemnity I must pay, if I promise you my friendship as well, or will you fix it yourself?

sp.speaker: Accuser
sp.p: Fix it; I like neither lawsuits nor disputes.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: A man of Sybaris fell from his chariot and wounded his head most severely; he was a very poor driver. One of his friends came up to him and said, "Every man to his trade." Well then, go you to Pittalus to get mended.

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: You are incorrigible.

sp.speaker: Accuser
sp.p: At all events, make a note of his reply.

div.stage: They start to leave.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Listen, instead of going off so abruptly. A woman at Sybaris broke a box.

sp.speaker: Accuser
sp.p: I again ask you to witness this.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: The box therefore had the fact attested, but the woman said, "Never worry about witnessing the matter, but hurry off to buy a cord to tie it together with; that will be the more sensible course."

sp.speaker: Accuser
sp.p: Oh! go on with your ribaldry until the Archon calls the case.

div.stage: He and his witness depart.

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: By Demeter! you'll stay here no longer! I am going to take you and carry you off.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: And what for?

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: What for? I am going to carry you into the house, so that the accusers will not run out of witnesses.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: One day at Delphi, Aesop ...

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: I don't care a fig for that.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: ... was accused of having stolen a sacred vase. But he replied, that the horn-beetle ...

sp.speaker: Bdelycleon
sp.p: Oh, dear, dear! You'll drive me crazy with your horn-beetle.

div.stage: Philocleon goes on with his fable while Bdelycleon is carrying him off the scene by main force.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: I envy you your happiness, old man. What a contrast to his former frugal habits and his very hard life! Taught now in quite another school, he will know nothing but the pleasures of ease. Perhaps he will jibe at it, for indeed it is difficult to renounce what has become one's second nature. However, many have done it, and adopting the ideas of others, have changed their use and wont.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: As for Philocleon's son, I, like all wise and judicious men, cannot sufficiently praise his filial tenderness and his tact. Never have I met a more amiable nature, and I have conceived the greatest fondness for him. How he triumphed on every point in his discussion with his father, when he wanted to bring him back to more worthy and honourable tastes!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.p: By Bacchus! Some Evil Genius has brought this unbearable disorder into our house. The old man, full up with wine and excited by the sound of the flute, is so delighted, so enraptured, that he is spending the night executing the old dances that Thespis first produced on the stage, and just now he offered to prove to the modern tragedians, by disputing with them for the dancing prize, that they are nothing but a lot of old dotards.

div.stage: Bdelycleon comes out of the house with his father who is costumed as Polyphemus in Euripides' Cyclops.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: "Who loiters at the door of the vestibule?"

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.p: Here comes our pest, our plague!

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Let down the barriers. The dance is now to begin.
sp.stage: He begins to dance in a manner grotesquely parodying that of Euripides.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.p: Or rather the madness.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Impetuous movement already twists and racks my sides. How my nostrils wheeze! how my back cracks!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.p: Go and fill yourself with hellebore.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Phrynichus is as bold as a cock and terrifies his rivals.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.p: He'll be stoned.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: His leg kicks out sky-high ...

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.p: ... and his arse gapes open.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Mind your own business. Look how easily my leg-joints move. Isn't that good?

sp.speaker: Bdedycleon
sp.p: God, no, it's merely insane!

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: And now I summon and challenge my rivals. If there be a tragic poet who pretends to be a skilful dancer, let him come and contest the matter with me. Is there one? Is there not one?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.p: Here comes one, and one only.

div.stage: A very small dancer, costumed as a crab, enters.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Who is the wretch?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.p: The younger son of Carcinus.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: I will crush him to nothing; in point of keeping time, I will knock him out, for he knows nothing of rhythm.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.p: Ah! ah! here comes his brother too, another tragedian, and another son of Carcinus.

div.stage: Another dancer, hardly larger than the first, and similarly costumed, enters.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Him I will devour for my dinner.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.p: Oh! ye gods! I see nothing but crabs. Here is yet another son of Carcinus.

div.stage: A third dancer enters, likewise resembling a crab, but smaller than either of the others.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: What's this? A shrimp or a spider?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.p: It's a crab, —a hermit-crab, the smallest of its kind; it writes tragedies.

sp.speaker: Philocleon
sp.p: Oh! Carcinus, how proud you should be of your brood! What a crowd of kinglets have come swooping down here! But we shall have to measure ourselves against them. Have marinade prepared for seasoning them, in case I prove the victor.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Let us stand out of the way a little, so that they may twirl at their ease.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.stage: It divides in two and accompanies with its song the wild dancing of Philocleon and the sons of Carcinus in the centre of the Orchestra.
sp.p: Come, illustrious children of this inhabitant of the brine, brothers of the shrimps,

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: skip on the sand and the shore of the barren sea; show us the lightning whirls and twirls of your nimble limbs. Glorious offspring of Phrynichus, let fly your kicks, so that the spectators may be overjoyed at seeing your legs so high in air.

Twist, twirl, tap your bellies, kick your legs to the sky. Here comes your famous father, the ruler of the sea, delighted to see his three lecherous kinglets. Go on with your dancing, if it pleases you, but as for us, we shall not join you. Lead us promptly off the stage, for never a comedy yet was seen where the Chorus finished off with a dance.
